paragraphs: To discover the rules of society best suited to nations, a superior intelligence would be needed, one that could see all the passions of men without feeling any of them. It would have to be wholly unrelated to our nature while knowing it through and through; its happiness would have to be independent of ours, yet it would have to be willing to concern itself with ours; and finally, it would have to look ahead to a distant glory across the passing of time, working in one century and able to enjoy the results in the next.[1] It would take gods to give men laws.

What Caligula argued from the facts, Plato argued from right in his dialogue the _Politicus_, in defining the civil or kingly man. But if great princes are rare, how much rarer are great legislators? The princes have only to follow the pattern that the legislators must lay down. The legislator is the engineer who invents the machine; the prince is merely the mechanic who sets it up and makes it run. “At the birth of societies,” says Montesquieu, “the rulers of Republics establish institutions, and afterwards the institutions shape the rulers.”[2]

Whoever dares to undertake the making of a people’s institutions ought to feel capable, so to speak, of changing human nature: of transforming each individual, who is by himself a complete and solitary whole, into part of a greater whole from which he in a sense receives his life and being; of altering man’s constitution so as to strengthen it; and of substituting a partial, moral existence for the physical and independent existence nature has given us all. In a word, he must take away from man his own resources and give him instead new ones that are foreign to him and cannot be used without the help of other men. The more completely these natural resources are wiped out, the greater and more lasting are the ones he acquires, and the more stable and perfect the new institutions. So if each citizen is nothing and can do nothing without the rest, and the resources acquired by the whole equal or exceed the sum of the resources of all the individuals, it may be said that legislation has reached the highest possible point of perfection.

The legislator holds an extraordinary position in the State in every respect. If he does so by reason of his genius, he does so no less by reason of his office, which is neither magistracy nor Sovereignty. This office, which sets up the Republic, does not enter into its constitution anywhere; it is a unique and superior function that has nothing in common with human authority. For if he who commands men ought not to command the laws, he who commands the laws ought not to command men either; otherwise his laws would be the servants of his passions and would often only serve to perpetuate his injustices, and his private aims would inevitably spoil the sanctity of his work.

When Lycurgus gave laws to his country, he began by resigning the throne. Most Greek towns had the custom of entrusting the establishment of their laws to foreigners. The Republics of modern Italy often followed this example; Geneva did the same and benefited from it.[3] Rome, at the height of its prosperity, saw all the crimes of tyranny revive and was brought to the brink of destruction, because it placed legislative authority and sovereign power in the same hands.

Nevertheless, the decemvirs themselves never claimed the right to pass any law on their own authority alone. “Nothing we propose to you,” they said to the people, “can pass into law without your consent. Romans, be yourselves the authors of the laws that are to make you happy.”

He, therefore, who draws up the laws has no right of legislation, or should have none; and the people cannot, even if it wishes, strip itself of this right that cannot be handed over, because, according to the fundamental compact, only the general will can bind the individuals, and there can be no assurance that a particular will conforms to the general will until it has been put to the free vote of the people. I have said this already, but it is worth repeating.
Thus in the task of legislation we find together two things that seem incompatible: an enterprise too difficult for human powers, and, for carrying it out, an authority that is no authority.

There is a further difficulty that deserves attention. Wise men who try to speak to the common herd in their own language instead of the herd’s cannot possibly make themselves understood. There are a thousand kinds of ideas that cannot be translated into popular language. Ideas that are too general and objects that are too remote are equally beyond its range. Each individual, having no taste for any plan of government except the one that suits his particular interest, finds it hard to see the advantages he might hope to draw from the continual privations that good laws impose. For a young people to be able to appreciate sound principles of political theory and follow the fundamental rules of statecraft, the effect would have to become the cause; the social spirit, which should be created by these institutions, would have to preside over their very foundation; and men would have to be, before law, what they are to become by means of law. The legislator therefore, being unable to appeal to either force or reason, must resort to an authority of a different kind, one capable of constraining without violence and persuading without convincing.

This is what has, in every age, forced the founders of nations to resort to divine intervention and to credit the gods with their own wisdom, so that the peoples, submitting to the laws of the State as to the laws of nature, and recognizing the same power in the formation of the city as in the formation of man, might obey freely and bear the yoke of the public happiness with docility.

This sublime reason, far above the reach of the common herd, is the reason whose decisions the legislator puts into the mouths of the immortals, so as to constrain by divine authority those whom human prudence could not move.[4] But not just anybody can make the gods speak, or get himself believed when he announces himself as their interpreter. The great soul of the legislator is the only miracle that can prove his mission. Any man can carve tablets of stone, or buy an oracle, or pretend to have secret dealings with some divinity, or train a bird to whisper in his ear, or find other crude ways of imposing on the people. A man whose knowledge goes no further may perhaps gather a band of fools around him; but he will never found an empire, and his extravagances will quickly perish with him. Idle tricks form a passing bond; only wisdom can make it lasting. The Judaic law, which still survives, and the law of the child of Ishmael, which for ten centuries has ruled half the world, still proclaim the great men who laid them down. And while the pride of philosophy or the blind spirit of faction sees in them nothing more than lucky impostures, the true political theorist admires, in the institutions they set up, the great and powerful genius that presides over things made to endure.

We should not conclude from this, with Warburton, that politics and religion have a common object among us, but rather that in the first periods of nations, the one is used as an instrument for the other.
